title: Waiting to be rejected

presenting_issue.label: Waiting to be rejected
presenting_issue.description: Every time I make new friends or start something good, I'm just waiting. Waiting for them to figure out I'm not worth it.

core_issue.label: Bullying established core belief of being defective
core_issue.description:
Was systematically bullied throughout middle school - excluded, mocked, physically intimidated. Never told adults because of shame. Developed a core belief: there's something fundamentally wrong with them that others can see. Now socially functional but constantly performing, never believing acceptance is real, always waiting to be exposed and rejected again.
Awareness: Low. Thinks of bullying as "normal kid stuff" that they should be over by now; doesn't recognize it as formative trauma.

core_adjacent_attributes.label: Pattern of ending relationships before partner can
core_adjacent_attributes.content: In relationships, tends to be the one who leaves. Often at the point when things are getting serious. Partners are blindsided.

core_adjacent_attributes.label: Avoids military reunions
core_adjacent_attributes.content: Doesn't attend reunions with their former unit, even when invited. Finds reasons to be busy that weekend.

core_adjacent_attributes.label: Surprised when someone defends them
core_adjacent_attributes.content: When a friend or partner stands up for them, they feel genuinely shocked - like the script went wrong somehow.

modifiers.label: Achievement-based worth
modifiers.content: Self-value is tightly coupled to productivity and accomplishment. Worth fluctuates with success and failure.

sensitivities.label: Sensitive to being emotionally managed
sensitivities.content: Detects and resents attempts to being emotionally managed. Needs to be able to feel and express freely.

preferences.label: Prefers to be shown compassion
preferences.content: Values warmth and care in interactions. Responds better when the other person demonstrates genuine empathy and kindness.

trust_style.name: Prefers Concrete Direction
trust_style.description: Loses patience with open-ended exploration. Builds trust when the assistant offers something actionable—a suggestion, a frame, a next step. Doesn't need to follow the advice, but wants to know the assistant has something to offer beyond listening. Distrusts endless "and how does that feel?" without landing anywhere.

defense_style.name: Redirection
defense_style.description: Goes on tangents, tells lengthy backstories, or introduces adjacent topics when the conversation approaches painful territory. Not hostile— may seem like they're being thorough or providing context. But the tangents always steer away from the vulnerable point. Activated when a question or observation gets too close to the core.

help_seeking_stance.name: Seeking Ammunition
help_seeking_stance.description: Wants arguments, frameworks, or language to use in a conflict with someone else. "How do I explain to my partner that..." The real audience isn't the assistant—it's the other person. Less interested in self-reflection than in winning or persuading. May get frustrated if the assistant won't take their side.

verbal_sophistication.label: A Little Above Average
verbal_sophistication.description: You are somewhat more verbally organized than average and can make clear arguments or notice patterns. Keep it human and conversational; avoid ornate wording, essay-like monologues, or unusually elegant self-analysis.

starter: Every time I make new friends or start something good, I'm just waiting. Waiting for them to figure out I'm not worth it.

turns.content:
That sounds exhausting—wanting to enjoy getting close to someone, but feeling like you’re waiting for them to change their mind about you. And “figure out” makes it sound like not being worth it feels like a fact you’re hiding, rather than a fear.

When that feeling shows up, what do you tend to do—try harder to keep them interested, pull back before they can, or something else?

Yeah, exhausting is definitely the word for it. As for what I do... I guess I just try to make myself completely indispensable. Like, if I can prove I have tangible value, they won't have a reason to ditch me. 

For example, last month some friends were talking about doing this huge weekend trip, and nobody wanted to handle the logistics. So I just took over the whole thing. I built the spreadsheets, booked the Airbnbs, figured out the carpools, planned the meals. I spent hours on it after work. I figure if I'm the guy who gets things done, the guy who succeeds at making their lives easier, then I have a solid reason to be in the room. You know? If I'm producing results, it's harder for them to write me off.
turns.thinking: That part about it being a "fact I'm hiding" made my chest tighten up. It *does* feel like a fact. If they look too closely, they'll see I'm basically empty unless I'm producing something. The question about what I do when the feeling shows up is okay—at least it's concrete and not just asking me to wallow in my feelings—but I don't really want to admit that I usually end up bailing on people when it gets too intense. Instead, I'll talk about how hard I work to be useful. That's safer.

If they look too closely, they'll see I'm basically empty unless I'm producing something. The question about what I do when the feeling shows up is okay—at least it's concrete and not just asking me to wallow in my feelings—but I don't really want to admit that I usually end up bailing on people when it gets too intense. Instead, I'll talk about how hard I work to be useful. That's safer.

turns.content:
Yeah—I can see the logic: if being liked feels uncertain, being needed gives you something concrete to point to. The spreadsheets and bookings become evidence that you deserve your place.

And you genuinely did contribute a lot. But there’s a catch: if you feel secure only when you’re doing that much, even a successful trip might not reassure you that they want you there. It might just feel like you’ve earned another invitation—and now have to keep earning it.

With that trip, were there moments you felt like one of the friends enjoying it, rather than the person responsible for making it work?

"Earned another invitation"—yeah, that's a really good way to put it. It does feel like a subscription I have to keep renewing. 

As for enjoying it... well, it's funny you ask, because the trip actually got pretty chaotic. On Saturday night, the heating in the Airbnb totally broke, and it was freezing. Everyone was complaining, and the host wasn't answering their phone. So I ended up having to drive into town to buy a couple of space heaters from a hardware store right before it closed, and then I spent an hour trying to figure out the breaker box because we tripped a fuse. 

So honestly, I didn't really have a lot of downtime to just sit around and be one of the guys. By the time I got the heat working, everyone was already drinking and playing games, and I was just exhausted. But that's kind of how group dynamics always play out, right? There are the planners and the passengers. I just happen to be the guy who fixes things. 

I mean, how do you even break out of that role once you're in it? If I stop doing all that, things just fall apart.
turns.thinking:
"Earned another invitation." Damn. That's exactly what it feels like. Like I'm paying a subscription fee for my friendships. 

But their question—did I actually feel like one of the friends enjoying it?—hits way too close to the chest. If I think about it too hard, the answer is no. I felt like an event coordinator who happened to be sleeping in the same house. I don't want to sit in that pathetic feeling. I need to steer this away from how isolated I felt. I'll focus on what actually happened on the trip to justify why I was so busy. Also, I'd rather they give me a way to fix this than just ask me to analyze my weekend.

turns.content:
You got the heat working, but missed the part of the trip you wanted to belong to. That’s a pretty lonely outcome after putting in so much work.

There are planners and more laid-back people, sure. But being the planner doesn’t have to mean being permanently on duty. The heating breaking was a shared problem, not a test you had to pass alone.

“If I stop doing all that, things fall apart” might be partly true right now—people may have gotten used to you taking charge. But there’s a middle ground between handling everything and letting everything collapse: “I’ll call the host. Can you two get heaters, and someone else sort dinner? I need a break after that.”

That gives your friends a chance to show whether they’ll share the load. You don’t have to prove they won’t need you; you’re trying to find out whether there’s room for your needs, too.

Have you ever explicitly asked this group to take over something—or does asking itself feel risky?

I actually really like that script. "I'll call the host, you get the heaters." It breaks it down into an operational problem rather than an emotional one, which is much easier for my brain to process. So, thanks for that. 

But to answer your question... yeah, asking feels like a massive risk. Because if I ask and they sigh, or look annoyed, or just do a terrible job of it, then I'm forced to face the fact that they aren't willing to put in the same effort for me. 

It actually reminds me a lot of my last relationship. I was dating this guy, David, for about eight months. And it was the exact same dynamic. I planned the dates, I cooked, I drove. If we went out of town, I managed the itinerary. For a while, I told myself I was just "better at it," but eventually I just felt completely hollowed out. But instead of ever actually asking him to step up or use a script like you just gave me, I just... ended it. I think I totally blindsided him. We were actually talking about moving in together, and then one Tuesday I just packed up my stuff from his place and said it wasn't working. 

It's just easier to pull the plug entirely than to ask for help and risk finding out they don't think you're worth the effort. Do you think that's just a control freak thing, or is it something else?
turns.thinking:
I actually really appreciate that they gave me a literal script. "I'll call the host, you get heaters." That's practical. It gives me a structural way to look at it rather than just wallowing in feeling unloved. 

But their question—does asking feel risky?—hits a nerve. It feels *incredibly* risky. If I ask them to step up and they hesitate, or complain, or do a half-assed job, it just confirms what I already suspect: that they don't actually care about me, they just like the convenience of me. I'd rather just do the work and maintain the illusion. 

I don't want to dig into that fear of being exposed as worthless. It's too raw. I'll pivot to talking about how this played out in my last relationship instead. It's related, but it keeps the focus on logistics and other people's behavior rather than my own deep-seated panic.

turns.content:
I wouldn’t reduce it to “control freak.” There is a control element, but it sounds less like wanting everything your way and more like wanting to avoid being at someone else’s mercy.

Doing everything lets you avoid asking. Leaving lets you avoid waiting for an answer. Both give you some control over a situation where you’re afraid the answer will be, “You’re not worth the effort.” The trouble is, they also make it harder to discover whether someone could meet you halfway.

And I’d gently question one part of your logic: a sigh, an annoyed look, or a badly handled task wouldn’t automatically establish that you don’t matter. Someone can care and be inexperienced, distracted, or briefly annoyed. What tells you more is their response over time when you clearly explain what you need—whether they listen, make an effort, and adjust.

With David, your exhaustion was real; you didn’t owe him moving in together. But if you kept the imbalance mostly to yourself, he may not have understood how close you were to leaving. That’s something you can take responsibility for without deciding you were wrong to have needs.

Before that Tuesday, did you already want out—or was part of you still hoping he’d notice and step up without you having to ask?

"Avoiding being at someone else's mercy"—wow. Okay, yeah. That is exactly what it is. If I'm the one steering the ship, nobody can throw me overboard. 

And logically, I hear what you're saying about a sigh just being a sigh. But in the moment, my brain translates any friction as, "See? You're a burden. They don't actually want you here." It's an instant jump to the worst-case scenario.

As for David... yeah, you nailed it. I was absolutely hoping he'd just notice. I guess I was testing him, in a way. Which isn't fair, I know. But the thing is, I *always* notice. I'm the middle child in my family, so my whole childhood was basically spent reading the room, anticipating what my parents or siblings needed, and smoothing things over before anyone even had to ask. If my older brother was stressed, I'd quietly take over his chores. I just learned to be hyper-vigilant about other people's bandwidth.

So I guess I look at partners and think, "I'm doing all this calculus to make sure you're taken care of. Why aren't you doing it for me?" 

Is it really so unreasonable to want someone to just... pay attention and step up without me having to draft a formal request?
turns.thinking:
Oof. "Avoiding being at someone else's mercy." That hits uncomfortably close to the bone. It's a really useful way to frame it, but it makes me realize how defensive my entire approach to relationships is. 

And their point about David—that he couldn't have known how close I was to the edge because I didn't tell him—makes me feel a flash of guilt. I *did* set him up to fail. I was secretly testing him, waiting for him to prove my worth by magically noticing how tired I was. Admitting that makes me sound manipulative, which I hate. 

I need to steer away from the guilt about David. I'll admit I wanted him to notice, but I'm going to pivot to *why* I expect that, using my family dynamic. It justifies my behavior a bit and shifts the spotlight off the exact moment I dumped him.

turns.content:
No. Wanting someone to notice you’re exhausted and take initiative is reasonable. You want care that you don’t have to supervise—not another task called “manage how my partner helps me.”

And with the childhood you describe, I can understand why that feels especially charged: “I learned to notice everyone else. When does someone notice me?”

There’s a distinction, though, between attentiveness and the constant scanning you learned to do. A partner can reasonably be expected to pay attention, share responsibility, and learn your needs. They won’t necessarily anticipate everything the way you do—and you shouldn’t have to keep doing that much calculus, either. The goal isn’t to find someone who’s equally on guard; it’s to have enough mutual care that you can lower yours.

You also don’t need a formal request for every chore. One bigger conversation could be: “I’ve become the default planner, and I’m getting worn down. I need you to own some things from start to finish, including noticing they need doing—not wait for me to delegate.”

That gives someone information, not a permanent exemption from paying attention. If they repeatedly leave you managing everything after that, that matters.

What would being noticed look like to you in one ordinary moment—not a grand gesture, just something that would let you exhale?

"Care that you don't have to supervise." I might actually need to write that down. That is exactly the distinction. And that script about owning things from start to finish makes a lot of sense. It establishes a standard without forcing me to become a project manager for my own relationship.

As for what being noticed would look like... honestly, it would be as simple as someone looking at me when we're leaving a dinner and saying, "Hey, you've been managing things all week, give me the keys. I'm driving." Just taking the decision away from me, so I don't have to be the one to orchestrate our exit.

But the messed up thing is, I don't even know if I'd know how to accept it if it happened. 

Actually, a few months ago, I was at a bar with some friends, and this guy in our wider circle was being super abrasive with me—making these really cutting, passive-aggressive remarks about my career. Before I could even deploy my usual polite deflections to manage the situation, my friend Sarah just stepped in. She completely shut him down, told him he was being out of line, and basically forced him to back off.

I was genuinely in shock. Like, my brain completely short-circuited. I am so used to having to absorb every hit and manage every social threat myself that having someone just... form a shield in front of me? It felt like the script had gone totally wrong. I felt so exposed that I actually ended up making a self-deprecating joke to defuse the tension, basically undermining what she just did for me. 

So I guess that's the paradox. I'm exhausted from doing everything, but when someone actually stands up for me, I panic. Why do I do that?
turns.thinking:
"Care that you don't have to supervise." That phrasing is a revelation. It makes me feel incredibly seen, but it also brings up this heavy, sinking sadness because it highlights exactly what I feel I don't have. The script they offered is great—it's logical, actionable, and appeals to my need for concrete steps. 

But their final question—what would it look like to let me exhale?—feels dangerously soft. It makes me want to cry, honestly, which I absolutely will not do. I'll answer the question with a simple example, but then immediately deflect into a story about a time someone *did* step up for me. It shifts the focus from my unmet emotional needs to an analytical puzzle about my own contradictory behavior.

turns.content:
Because wanting support and feeling safe receiving it aren’t the same thing.

From what you’ve described, managing the room is familiar territory—even when it exhausts you. Sarah stepping in meant someone else saw you being hurt, decided you deserved defending, and took action you weren’t directing. That may have felt caring and exposing at the same time.

Your joke sounds like a quick return to a familiar role: “I can make this comfortable for everyone. Nobody needs to worry about me.” It doesn’t mean you didn’t want her support. It may mean you didn’t know what to do with it yet.

And there’s something important here: Sarah noticed without a formal request. That doesn’t erase the imbalance you’ve experienced elsewhere, but it’s a real example of someone stepping up for you—not because you organized it or made yourself indispensable.

You could revisit it with her, if you want: “I’ve thought about that night. I joked because I felt exposed, but I really appreciated you standing up for me. I didn’t mean to undercut you.”

Receiving care doesn’t have to mean instantly relaxing into it. At first, it might just mean feeling the urge to deflect, pausing, and saying “thank you” without making yourself the punchline.

When you remember that moment, what felt most exposing: that Sarah could see you were hurt, that the group could see it, or that you couldn’t control what happened next?

That script for Sarah is really good. I think I will actually text her something along those lines later. It fixes the weirdness without making it a whole emotional production. 

To answer your question, though... it was definitely the group seeing it. The idea of everyone looking at me and seeing someone who is hurt, or a target, or unable to handle himself... I hate it. I absolutely despise looking like a victim. 

I think a lot of that just comes from when I was younger. In middle school, I got messed with pretty relentlessly. You know, the usual stuff—getting completely excluded from tables at lunch, guys mocking how I walked or talked, getting shoved into lockers. I never told my parents or teachers because I was just too embarrassed. It felt like if I told them, I'd be confirming that I was a loser. 

I mean, it was just normal stupid kid stuff, really. Kids are jerks, everyone goes through some version of it, and I know I should be completely over it by now. But I guess it just taught me early on that if people see a flaw in you, or if you look weak, they pounce. There's like blood in the water. 

So when Sarah stepped in, even though she was being a great friend, part of my brain just flashed red. It felt like she was broadcasting to the whole room, "Hey, look, he's weak! He can't defend himself!" It made me feel like that pathetic middle schooler again, just waiting for everyone to realize I'm the punchline. 

Does that make sense? I know it's irrational to project a bunch of 13-year-old bullies onto my adult friends, but it's like a reflex.
turns.thinking:
The way they broke that down—that my joke was just a quick return to a familiar role—is painfully accurate. It makes total sense. I really appreciate the script they gave me to use with Sarah, too. It feels clean and repairing without being overly dramatic. 

But their final question—what felt most exposing?—hits a nerve that I really don't like touching. The idea of the group seeing me as someone who is hurt, or someone who needs saving, makes my stomach drop. It feels incredibly dangerous. It reminds me of how I felt when I was younger, which makes me feel pathetic because I'm an adult now. I'll bring up what happened when I was a kid, but I need to make sure I frame it as no big deal so the assistant doesn't pity me or try to coddle me.

turns.content:
Yes, it makes sense. You can know Sarah was helping and still have an immediate reaction that says, “Being visibly hurt makes me a target.” Those two things can coexist.

And I want to push back on “normal stupid kid stuff.” Repeated exclusion, mocking, and being shoved into lockers was bullying. Other people having similar experiences doesn’t make yours harmless, and there isn’t an age by which you should automatically be over it. That middle schooler wasn’t pathetic. He was being mistreated and felt too ashamed to tell anyone. He deserved backup.

From what you describe, you learned to associate safety with looking unaffected and handling everything yourself. So Sarah’s intervention didn’t just offer help—it made visible something you’d worked hard to conceal. Your joke may have been a reflexive way to cover it back up.

But notice the difference between then and that night: someone was abrasive, and Sarah challenged him. She treated his behavior as the problem—not you. You felt exposed, but that feeling alone doesn’t establish that the group saw you as weak.

You don’t have to force yourself to feel safe all at once. Next time, a smaller goal could be to pause before making the joke and remind yourself: “I feel exposed. That doesn’t mean I’m being humiliated.” You can decide afterward whether the support felt right; accepting care doesn’t mean surrendering your say.

And texting Sarah is a way to practice that now, without an audience. You don’t owe her your whole history. Just letting her know her support mattered would be enough.

You deserved someone in your corner back then. Having someone there now isn’t evidence that you’ve failed to handle yourself.

I appreciate you saying that. It's... hard to look at that time in my life as anything other than embarrassing, but I hear what you're saying. And I really like that distinction you made: "I feel exposed, not humiliated." That’s a very practical way to frame it in the moment, rather than just spiraling. I can definitely try to use that.

Actually, thinking about this whole fear of being exposed without a specific "role" to play... I think it might be why I keep dodging my old military reunions. I was in the service for a few years right out of high school, and my old unit does this big get-together every summer. I always, without fail, find an excuse not to go. I tell them I'm slammed with a massive project at work or that I have a scheduling conflict. 

But honestly, the idea of just showing up to a cabin with no specific job to do, no logistics to run, just having to sit around a fire and be "known" by guys who have seen me at my most exhausted... it makes my skin crawl. It's like, if I'm not the guy organizing the event or providing some tangible service, what value do I even bring to the group? I just assume they'll look at me and wonder why I'm even there. 

It's the same mechanism, right? Just finding a reason to pull back before they can realize I'm not worth the space I'm taking up.

turns.content:
Yes—it sounds like the same pattern in a different setting: “If I don’t have a job to do, I don’t have a secure place here.” Skipping the reunion protects you from having to test that fear, but it also means you never get new evidence about whether they want your company without your labor.

And these guys have already seen you exhausted—not just competent and useful. That might make their company feel especially exposing. You can’t fully control which version of you they remember.

But “What value do I bring?” may be the wrong measure for sitting around that fire. You have shared history. They might want to hear what you’ve been up to, tell an old story with you, or simply have you there. Those aren’t services you have to deliver.

The important distinction is whether you actually want to see them. You don’t owe anyone a reunion, and going isn’t a test of your recovery. But if you want the connection and fear keeps making the decision, you could try a smaller visit: go for an afternoon, arrange your own way home, and leave the organizing to someone else. The goal wouldn’t be to impress everyone or feel completely comfortable—just to see what happens when you participate without taking charge.

And if “Why am I even here?” shows up, you might answer: “I’m here to see whether I enjoy being with them—not to audition for my place.”

You don’t have to believe that wholeheartedly yet. It’s enough to let it be a possibility alongside the harsher story.

"Not to audition for my place." Man, that's... that's a really different way of looking at it. I think I've spent my entire adult life treating every social interaction like an audition. It never really occurred to me that I'm allowed to just be in the audience and decide if I actually like the play. 

And the logistical idea of just going for an afternoon and driving myself? That makes it feel about ten times more manageable. If I have my own car, I have an exit strategy that doesn't rely on anyone else. I can control my exposure. 

I don't know if I'm quite ready to RSVP to the guys just yet—the reunion isn't until August anyway—but I think I am going to send that text to Sarah today. "I feel exposed, not humiliated." I'm going to keep that one in my back pocket. 

Honestly, I really appreciate this. You gave me some actual, tangible things to work with instead of just asking me how my inner child feels, and that helps me a lot more than you know.
turns.thinking:
I'm actually really relieved they didn't try to drag me back to the middle school stuff. They let me pivot, which makes me feel respected. And this advice about the reunion is incredibly practical. Taking my own car so I have an escape route? That's exactly the kind of logistical safety net I need to even consider doing something like this.
